intro: The rulebook for how criminal cases run — FIRs, arrest, investigation, bail, trial and appeal. In force since 1 July 2024, replacing the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) of 1973. It adds e-FIRs, video recording of searches, forensic visits and timelines for investigations and trials.

sections.p: Information about a cognizable offence can be given orally, in writing, or electronically. You can file it at any police station regardless of where the crime happened ('Zero FIR'); it is then transferred. An e-FIR must be signed by the informant within 3 days. You get a free copy of the FIR. For offences punishable with 3–7 years, police may do a preliminary enquiry (within 14 days) before registering.
k: If police refuse, you can send the complaint to the Superintendent of Police (173(4)), and then approach a magistrate
Statements of women victims of certain sexual offences are recorded by a woman officer

sections.p: Police can investigate cognizable offences without a magistrate's order. If police don't act, a magistrate can order investigation on your application (175(3)) — usually after you've approached the SP.
For offences punishable with 7 years or more, a forensic team must visit the crime scene to collect evidence, and the process should be video-recorded on a mobile phone or other device.
Police can examine people who know the facts. You must answer truthfully but are not bound to answer questions that may incriminate you. Statements can be recorded by audio-video.

Confessions and statements are recorded by a magistrate, who must warn the person they're not bound to confess and that it may be used against them. A confession to police alone is not admissible (see BSA S 23).

sections.t: Medical exam of a rape victim
sections.p: A registered doctor must examine the victim within 24 hours of receiving information, with her consent, and send the report to the investigating officer within 7 days.

Investigation must finish without unnecessary delay. For rape and POCSO offences, it should be completed within 2 months. Police must update the victim/informant on progress within 90 days, including electronically.
Courts or police can summon any document, electronic communication or device that is needed for an investigation or trial.
Search and seizure — including preparing the list of seized items — must be recorded by audio-video, preferably on a mobile phone, and sent to the magistrate.
A court can attach and forfeit property derived from a crime, on application of the police.

Police can arrest without a warrant for cognizable offences in specified situations. For offences punishable with up to 7 years, police should usually issue a notice to appear instead of arresting, if conditions are met. People above 60 or infirm can't be arrested for offences punishable with less than 3 years without permission of an officer of DSP rank or above.
k: If you comply with a notice of appearance, you generally shouldn't be arrested

sections.p: The officer must wear a clear name tag and identification. An arrest memo must be prepared, attested by a family member or local witness, and signed by the arrested person.

A woman can't be arrested after sunset and before sunrise except in exceptional cases, with a woman officer and prior permission of a magistrate. Handcuffs may be used for habitual or repeat offenders, escapees, and those accused of serious crimes like organised crime, terrorism or murder.

sections.t: Right to know grounds and bail
sections.p: You must be told the full grounds of arrest immediately. If the offence is bailable, you must be told you have the right to bail and can arrange sureties.
Police must inform a relative, friend or person you nominate about your arrest and where you're held. Details are displayed at the police station and district control room.
You can't be held in police custody for more than 24 hours (excluding travel time) without being produced before a magistrate.

A magistrate can allow police custody of up to 15 days in total, which may be taken in parts during the first 40 days (offences up to 10 years) or 60 days (more serious offences). Total detention without chargesheet is capped at 60 or 90 days — after that you get 'default bail'.
For bailable offences, bail is a right. The police officer or court must release you on bail (or a bond, if you can't afford it).

An undertrial who has spent half the maximum sentence in jail must be released on bail. A first-time offender must be released after one-third. Not for offences punishable by death or life imprisonment. Jail superintendents must apply on their behalf.

Courts can grant bail in non-bailable offences, but not usually where there are reasonable grounds to believe the person committed an offence punishable with death or life. Women, children under 16, and the sick or infirm get special consideration.
If you fear arrest for a non-bailable offence, you can apply to the Sessions Court or High Court for anticipatory bail — if granted, you're released on bail if arrested.

sections.t: Bail powers of High Court and Sessions Court
sections.p: These courts have wider powers to grant bail and to set aside or modify conditions imposed by a magistrate.
You can file a criminal complaint directly with a magistrate. The magistrate examines you and witnesses on oath, and must give the accused a chance to be heard before taking cognizance.
The accused and victim (if represented) must be given copies of the police report and documents within 14 days of first appearance, including electronically.
In Sessions trials, charges should be framed within 60 days of the first hearing on charge.
Judgment should be delivered within 30 days of arguments ending, extendable to 45 days for specific reasons.
If a proclaimed offender absconds to avoid trial, the trial can proceed and judgment be given in their absence, after following specified safeguards.
Every state must have a witness protection scheme to protect witnesses from threats.
Trials, inquiries, summons, examination of witnesses and appeals can be held in electronic mode, including video-conferencing.

sections.t: Maintenance of wives, children and parents
sections.p: A person with enough means who neglects or refuses to maintain their wife, children or parents who can't maintain themselves can be ordered by a magistrate to pay monthly maintenance. Applies regardless of religion.

A District Magistrate or other executive magistrate can issue urgent orders (e.g. banning gatherings) to prevent danger, obstruction or disturbance of public peace. Orders last up to 2 months, extendable by the state to 6 months.
An executive magistrate can require someone likely to disturb the peace to sign a bond to keep the peace for up to a year.
High Courts can make any order needed to prevent abuse of the court's process or to secure justice — commonly used to quash FIRs or criminal proceedings.
